chunks.text: Library Letter · May 10, twenty twenty-six · 5 min read · By Don Goldstein

Search results aren’t ten blue links anymore. They’re a paragraph Google wrote, citing two or three sources, and for restaurant queries that paragraph now appears above the map pack. The nine pieces below are the operator’s response to that shift, in the order to read them.
In short

Week 1 of a new editorial cadence, nine pieces shipped together as a Sunday-night-through-Monday-morning batch, English and Spanish, anchored to publicly-verifiable platform docs, vendor pricing, and search-industry analyses.

Through-line: search results aren’t ten blue links anymore, they’re a paragraph Google wrote, citing two or three sources. For restaurant queries that paragraph now appears above the map pack, and if you’re not one of the cited sources, you’re not in the conversation.

Read the AI Overview citation piece first; the other eight ladder from it in this order: schema example, GMaps invisibility, review playbook, Instagram-as-S E O, three-platform delivery math, the 30-day case study, loyalty programs, service charges vs tipping.

Week 1 of a new batch cadence. This week is bigger than usual because it lays down the foundation the next ones will build on. Future batches will hook to whatever’s moving in the restaurant industry that week, a Google product update, a delivery-platform policy change, a wage-law phase-in. AI Overview citation is the new discovery surface, and almost no independent restaurant writes for it yet.
The through-line.

Two things are happening at the same time, and they compound. One: Google’s search-result page is a paragraph the model wrote, citing two or three sources. As of March twenty twenty-five it triggered on 13.14% of US desktop searches; by spring twenty twenty-six it’s approaching one in five, and restaurant queries trigger it more often than the average. Two: the map pack still sits beneath that paragraph, and it’s still where most local-intent traffic clicks. So you’re competing on two surfaces at once, one new and shaped by paragraph quality, one old and shaped by Google Business Profile health.

AI Overview share of US desktop search, climbing across three readings, with a tick on each bar marking where the measure stood in January twenty twenty-five so the slope is visible. In January twenty twenty-five it was six point four nine percent of US desktop queries. By March twenty twenty-five it had roughly doubled to thirteen point one four percent, the most-cited measurement. By spring twenty twenty-six the share is approaching one in five queries, about twenty percent, and restaurant queries trigger it above the all-categories average. The tick on the later bars sits back at the January six point four nine starting point, so the eye reads the gain directly. The wave ships now because the gap between operators who write citation-shaped pages and those who do not is the widest it will be.

Five of the nine pieces address those two surfaces directly. The remaining four address the operating-economics decisions that determine what your restaurant actually has to say on those surfaces, what your menu costs to put in front of a guest, who handles the discovery, what compensation model your kitchen runs on.

Before the reading order, the one test the whole wave is built around: when the model drafts that paragraph and reaches for two or three sources, is your page one it can actually lift from? Walk the three questions.

A decision tree for whether your page is citation-shaped, the single test the nine-piece wave is built around. First question: does a single paragraph on your page answer one specific diner question in plain text, like where to get carbonara in your neighborhood? If no, the model has nothing clean to lift and quotes a competitor who wrote it down; that is the fix the thesis piece teaches. If yes, you have a candidate paragraph. Second question: can a machine read your key facts, cuisine, hours, location, price, without a human looking at the photo? If those facts live only in a photographed menu or a P D F, the model cannot parse them, which is the gap the schema-markup companion closes. Third question: do your reviews and profile back the claim up, so the model trusts the source it is about to cite? If the rating is thin or the newest review is old, the model hesitates, which is why the review-response playbook sits in the first band. Clear all three and you are a citable source; miss any one and you are furniture below the answer. The verdict pill on each branch names the outcome.
The reading order.

Each piece stands alone, but they ladder. Read them in order, the role tag on each tile tells you why the piece sits where it does. Search citation first (one through four), then social discovery (five), then operations and economics (six through nine).

The wave reads in three bands. Band one is search citation, pieces one through four. Start with the thesis on paragraph-shape rules for AI Overview citation; then the technical companion on restaurant schema markup; then the diagnostic on Google Maps invisibility; then the operator playbook on Google review responses. Band two is social discovery, piece five is the Instagram-as-S E O operator strategy. Band three is operations and economics, pieces six through nine: the three-platform delivery math, the thirty-day post-delisting playbook, the loyalty-program R O I walk, and the service-charge versus tipping model. Each band hands the operator a different lever; reading in order is what shows how the levers compound.
Read the wave
In order, with role.
01 Thesis How to get cited in Google’s AI Overview The paragraph-shape rules that turn a page into a cited source. Read first, every other piece ladders from this one.
02 Technical companion Restaurant schema markup, paste-ready The Json-LD block that gives number 01 the entity scaffolding to cite. Six types, seven editable fields, validation step at the end.
03 Diagnostic My restaurant isn’t on Google Maps The 10-minute walk for restaurants that don’t appear in the map pack. Four root causes; three are operator-fixable same day.
04 Review playbook How to respond to Google reviews Four review archetypes, four response shapes. The 3-star is the most-read, that’s where undecided guests calibrate.
05 Social discovery Instagram as restaurant S E O Google indexes captions; the in-app search bar is a discovery surface most independents still write at like it’s twenty nineteen.
06 Channel math Uber Eats vs DoorDash vs Grubhub Same 42 dollars ticket, three side-by-side margin walks. The headline 30% commission is identical; the second-layer fee stack opens a real spread.
07 Delisting playbook 30 days after leaving DoorDash The week-by-week shape of a delisting: which costs flex, which complaints arrive, where the channel mix lands. Pairs with number 06.
08 Retention math Loyalty programs that pay Four models, vendor-published prices, where each one wins. The loyalty conversation is downstream of the channel conversation.
09 Compensation math Service charges vs tipping Three models, one 200 dollars check. Server take-home varies; operator net varies; the customer pays about the same and feels differently about each.
Search citation · Social discovery · Operations & economics
What the claims in these pieces are anchored to.

Every operating-floor number across the nine articles is anchored to a publicly verifiable source, platform-published commission tiers, vendor pricing pages, search-industry analyses, and Google’s own help documentation, or to an illustrative range that’s identified as such in the piece itself. Specific anchors include:

Platform commission and fee structures. DoorDash Marketplace tiers (Basic 15% / Plus 25% / Premier 30%), Uber Eats and Grubhub published rates, payment-processing rates, all from the platforms’ own merchant documentation. Powers the DoorDash margin walk, the three-platform comparison, the 30-day playbook.

AI Overview share of US search. The March twenty twenty-five Search Engine Land analysis (13.14% of US desktop queries) is the most-cited measurement; subsequent direction is qualitative. Powers the AI Overview citation article’s framing.

Loyalty + email vendor pricing. Toast Rewards, Square Loyalty, Fivestars/Como, Mailchimp, Klaviyo monthly costs are taken from each vendor’s current public pricing page. Powers the loyalty comparison.
Dmv Google Business Profile audit (twenty twenty-three, twenty twenty-six). Sample of independent restaurants in the Dmv; source for the four root causes of map-pack invisibility in piece number 3.
Don Goldstein is a restaurant operator and runs Muntin Digital . He writes the weekly batches that ship on this page.
Key takeaways
Nine pieces, three operating themes: search citation (4 pieces), social discovery (1), delivery economics and operations (4).

Operating-floor claims across the wave are anchored to publicly-verifiable sources: platform commission tiers from each platform’s merchant docs, vendor pricing from each vendor’s pricing page, AI Overview share from the March twenty twenty-five Search Engine Land analysis.
Future batches will mostly be smaller and hook to current events (Google updates, delivery-platform policy changes, wage-law inflections) rather than calendar.
All ten pieces ship audio in six languages, English, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, Mandarin.
Single operating principle: ranking and being cited are not the same job, the first restaurant in a market to write for the citation owns the answer box for the next twelve months.
